extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia entry describing Gauss's Class Number Problem: the task of determining fundamental discriminants of binary quadratic forms having a given class number, the special case of class number one (Heegner numbers), and the history of results and proofs. Includes references to major contributions and computational results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of Gauss's Class Number Problem
rubrics_metrics.description: For a given , determine a complete list of fundamental binary quadratic form discriminants such that the class number is given by .
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central problem the article addresses: identify, for each specified class number h, all fundamental discriminants d (of primitive binary quadratic forms / corresponding imaginary quadratic fields) whose class number equals h. The entry frames subsequent historical results and solved cases in terms of this problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / identification of Heegner numbers (class number one)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conway and Guy (1996) call the nine values of  having  where  is the binary quadratic form discriminant corresponding to an  quadratic field (...) the Heegner numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These nine discriminants (the Heegner numbers) are the complete solution to Gauss's problem for class number 1. The entry cites OEIS A003173 and notes that the Heegner numbers have a number of fascinating properties. (Original page lists the nine discriminants explicitly; in context these are the discriminants corresponding to the imaginary quadratic fields with class number one.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical acceptance and independent verifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Heegner (1952) gave a solution for , but it was not completely accepted due to a number of apparent gaps. However, subsequent examination of Heegner's proof showed it to be 'essentially' correct (Conway and Guy 1996). Stark (1967) and Baker (1966) gave independent proofs of the fact that only nine such numbers exist; both proofs were accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry emphasizes the chronology and acceptance of proofs: Heegner's original 1952 work, later independent verifications by Stark and Baker establishing uniqueness of the nine class-number-one discriminants, and the subsequent resolution of prior objections.
